passages.happening:
“You are to build an altar of acacia wood. The altar must be square, five cubits long, five cubits wide, and three cubits high” (verse 1). “Make a horn on each of its four corners, so that the horns are of one piece, and overlay it with bronze” (verse 2).

Its tools are of bronze: pots for the ashes, shovels, sprinkling bowls, meat forks and firepans (verse 3). A bronze grate sits halfway up (verses 4-5). Poles carry it (verses 6-7). “Construct the altar with boards so that it is hollow. It is to be made just as you were shown on the mountain” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 25 and 26 moved from the ark outward to the tent. Chapter 27 steps outside the tent into the courtyard, the space ordinary Israelites could enter.

The bronze altar stood between the gate and the tent. No one could come near the dwelling of God without passing the place of sacrifice. It was the largest object in the sanctuary, about 7.5 feet or 2.3 meters square and 4.5 feet or 1.4 meters high, and the first thing a worshiper met inside the gate. The Hebrew word for altar, mizbeach, comes from the verb for slaughtering a sacrifice.

Look at the tools: pots for ashes, shovels, bowls for the blood, forks for the meat, pans for the fire. This was not a quiet shrine. It was a working hearth of worship, with fire, blood and smoke. The offerings of Leviticus 1 to 7 would be made here.

The horns on its corners were its most holy points. The priest put blood from the sin offering on them. And a man fleeing for his life could take hold of them to claim protection. Archaeologists have found horned altars from ancient Israel, at Megiddo and at Beersheba.
passages.later:
Leviticus says the priest is to put blood of the sin offering “on the horns of the altar of burnt offering” (Leviticus 4:25). Adonijah, afraid of Solomon, “went to take hold of the horns of the altar” (1 Kings 1:50).

Hebrews contrasts the daily sacrifices with Christ: “Day after day every priest stands to minister and to offer again and again the same sacrifices”, “But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God” (Hebrews 10:11-12). And it says, “We have an altar” (Hebrews 13:10), for “Jesus also suffered outside the city gate, to sanctify the people by His own blood” (Hebrews 13:12).

That line between the altar and the cross is the New Testament's own. It is not a code hidden in the boards of this chapter. It is the claim that what the altar did again and again, Christ did once.
passages.hard:
How does a wooden altar covered in bronze fit the command in 20:24-25 for an altar of earth or uncut stone?

Several answers are given. Many interpreters, ancient and modern, suggest that the hollow frame of verse 8 was filled with earth or rough stones wherever it was set up, so that the fire burned on earth and the bronze box was a casing to carry it. On this reading the two laws describe one altar. Others take 20:24-25 as the rule for the simple altars built in many places, as Joshua built one of uncut stones, while chapter 27 governs the one altar of the central sanctuary. Critical scholars often assign the two laws to different sources and periods.

These notes take no side. Both texts share one concern: the altar is built on God's terms, not as a display of human skill or power.
passages.asks: No one could reach the tent without passing the altar. Ask whether you want to come near God without facing the cost of sin. And ask what it means to you that, in the New Testament's words, Christ offered one sacrifice for all time.

passages.happening:
“You are also to make a courtyard for the tabernacle” (verse 9). Linen curtains hang on posts with bronze bases and silver hooks and bands: a hundred cubits on the south side and on the north, fifty on the west (verses 9-12). The east side, “toward the sunrise”, has curtains on either side of a gate (verses 13-15).

“The gate of the courtyard shall be twenty cubits long, with a curtain embroidered with blue, purple, and scarlet yarn, and finely spun linen” (verse 16).

“The entire courtyard shall be a hundred cubits long and fifty cubits wide, with curtains of finely spun linen five cubits high” (verse 18). All the tent pegs are of bronze (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The courtyard section reads like a surveyor's plan. It walks round the edge, south, north, west and east, and then gives the totals.

The courtyard was about 150 by 75 feet, or 46 by 23 meters. Its curtains stood about 7.5 feet high, too tall to see over. So the sanctuary was hidden from the camp until a person came in through the gate.

There was one gate, on the east, wide and colorful, in the same blue, purple and scarlet as the veil inside.

Notice the tent pegs of verse 19. This was a camp. It was taken down and pitched again every time Israel moved.
passages.later: The psalms speak of longing for these courts: “My soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the LORD” (Psalm 84:2), and “Enter His gates with thanksgiving and His courts with praise” (Psalm 100:4).
passages.asks: The courtyard had one gate, and it faced the sunrise. Ask with what attitude you come into God's presence: with thanksgiving, or only with requests. And ask whether you long for God's house the way the psalm-writer did.

passages.happening:
“And you are to command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually” (verse 20).

“In the Tent of Meeting, outside the veil that is in front of the Testimony, Aaron and his sons are to tend the lamps before the LORD from evening until morning. This is to be a permanent statute for the Israelites for the generations to come” (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The chapter turns back inside to the lamps, and for the first time in these chapters it names who will serve: Aaron and his sons. That leads straight into the next two chapters, on the priests' clothing and their ordination.

‘Pure oil of pressed olives’ is, word for word, beaten oil. The olives were crushed lightly rather than pressed hard. That gave the first and clearest oil, which burned brightly with little smoke. It was costly, and it was to come from the whole people. Every household had a share in the light that burned before God through the night.

‘Continually’ is tamid. Verse 21 says what it means: from evening until morning, night after night. It describes a regular, faithful practice. The same word is used for the daily offering and for the bread on the table.

This is also the first time the Bible uses the name Tent of Meeting, which becomes the tabernacle's most common name.
passages.later:
Leviticus repeats the command: “Command the Israelites to bring you pure oil of pressed olives for the light, to keep the lamps burning continually” (Leviticus 24:2).

Jesus told his followers, “You are the light of the world” (Matthew 5:14). In Revelation the risen Christ warns a church that will not turn back, “I will come to you and remove your lampstand from its place” (Revelation 2:5).
passages.asks: The lamps burned night after night because someone tended them, with oil the whole people brought. Ask what you bring to the life of your church that others depend on. And ask what keeps your own faith burning through the night, when no one sees.
